summary: Defines the Robust Header Compression framework, a way to shrink packet headers efficiently over links with different characteristics. It separates the framework and the profile for uncompressed packets from the original definition in RFC 3095. It is a proposed standard that replaced RFC 4995.

plainLanguage.summary: When the same long address label is on every box, you agree on a short nickname after the first one, so later boxes carry less writing.

subtitle: The common rulebook for squeezing IP, UDP, RTP and TCP headers over links that lose and corrupt packets.

tldr.problem: Packet headers repeat the same information in every packet of a flow, which wastes bandwidth on expensive links. Older compression schemes did poorly on lossy links with long round-trip times.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC keeps matching state (a context) at both ends of a link and sends only what changed, tagged with a context identifier. The framework defines the channel, packet types, feedback, segmentation and CRCs that every compression profile shares.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5795 states the framework separately from the profiles, replaces RFC 4995 and fixes one interoperability error in how the feedback Size field was described.

today: RFC 5795 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4995. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Compress Headers
sections.content:
On some links the headers cost more than the data. An application sending RTP over IPv4 carries an IPv4 header (20 octets), a UDP header (8 octets) and an RTP header (12 octets), a total of 40 octets. With IPv6 the IPv6 header is 40 octets, for a total of 60. For Voice over IP, the coded speech can be as small as 15-20 octets, so the saving is large.

Compression works because most header fields barely change between packets of the same flow. The Robust Header Compression (ROHC) protocol is meant to work efficiently and robustly over different link technologies. Older schemes such as those in RFC 2507 and RFC 2508 performed inadequately where the link is lossy and the round-trip time is not negligible, as on wireless links and IP tunnels.

The framework and a first set of profiles were defined together in RFC 3095. This document defines the framework on its own, together with the profile for uncompressed packets. It does not modify the framework of RFC 3095, and implementations based on either definition interoperate. The intent is that this text replaces RFC 3095 as the base for all future profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending the full address on every packet is like writing your whole home address on every postcard to the same friend. ROHC lets you write it once and then use a short code.

sections.title: How Earlier Schemes Fell Short
sections.content:
The RFC gives a short history. The first scheme, compressed TCP (CTCP, often called VJ compression and defined in RFC 1144), shrinks the 40 octets of a TCP/IP header to 4 octets using delta encoding. IP header compression (RFC 2507) handles arbitrary IP, TCP and UDP headers but does not compress RTP. CRTP (RFC 2508) compresses the 40 octets of IPv4/UDP/RTP headers to a minimum of 2 octets when the UDP checksum is not enabled.

The weakness is loss. On lossy links with long round-trip times, each packet lost makes several following packets fail to decompress, because the context stays invalid for at least one link round-trip time. The large headers sent to repair the context then waste more bandwidth. The enhanced variant eCRTP (RFC 3545) added robustness at the cost of extra overhead and lower efficiency.

The RFC names three properties by which a scheme is judged: compression efficiency (how much the average header shrinks), robustness (tolerating loss, residual bit errors and reordering without causing extra damage) and transparency (whether decompressed headers are bitwise identical to the originals). More robustness always costs some efficiency, and the reverse.
sections.plainLanguage: Old shortcuts worked only if no mail was ever lost. When a letter went missing, everyone got confused and had to start over. ROHC is built to keep going even when something goes missing.

sections.title: Contexts, Flows and Profiles
sections.content:
Packets are grouped into flows, usually by source and destination address, transport protocol and ports. The compressor and decompressor each keep a context for a flow, the state used to compress or decompress its headers, and identify it with a Context Identifier (CID) carried in each compressed header. The context has a static part (fields classified STATIC, STATIC-KNOWN or STATIC-DEF) and a dynamic part (fields classified CHANGING). Fields are also classed as INFERRED when they can be worked out from elsewhere, such as the frame size from the link layer.

Changing fields are compressed as a function of a master sequence number (MSN), which is either taken from a protocol field such as the RTP sequence number or created by the compressor. When a field stops following its function, extra information is sent to update the function.

A profile is a compression protocol for a specific combination of headers. Each has a unique profile identifier, and the set supported by both ends of the channel is negotiated. A ROHC channel is a logical unidirectional point-to-point channel from one compressor to one decompressor. It may also carry feedback for a channel in the opposite direction.

The CID space is either small (values 0 through 15) or large (0 through 16383). Which one is used MUST be established before any compressed packet is sent. The CID space is separate for each channel, so CID 3 on channel A and CID 3 on channel B are different contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: Each conversation gets a number, like a table number at a restaurant. Both sides keep notes under that number, so they do not have to repeat everything each time.

sections.title: ROHC Packets and Packet Types
sections.content:
A ROHC packet is made of optional Padding octets, optional Feedback elements, at most one Header and then the Payload. At least one of Feedback or Header MUST be present. The Header is a profile-specific compressed header, an IR or IR-DYN header, or a segment.

The framework reserves a few packet types by their leading bits and leaves the rest to profiles. With small CIDs, CID 0 costs no bits at all, and CIDs 1 to 15 use an Add-CID octet before the packet type. With large CIDs the CID is always present, encoded in one or two octets using the self-describing variable-length scheme.

Two packet types set up contexts. The IR (Initialization and Refresh) header associates a CID with a profile and typically initializes the context. The IR-DYN header can never initialize a context that has not been initialized, but it can redefine the profile of a context if that profile allows it. Both carry an 8-bit profile field (the 8 least significant bits of the profile identifier) and an 8-bit CRC.

Initially, every context is in a no context state. If the 8-bit CRC of an IR or IR-DYN packet fails, the packet MUST NOT be decompressed and delivered. If a parsing error occurs for any packet type, the decompressor MUST discard the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet starts with a tiny label that says what kind it is. Some labels start a new conversation, and some just carry the short version.

sections.title: Feedback, Segmentation and the Uncompressed Profile
sections.content:
Feedback carries information from the decompressor back to the compressor. There are three categories: an ACK (decompression succeeded and the context is considered valid), a NACK (some or all of the dynamic context is considered invalid) and a STATIC-NACK (the entire static context is invalid or not established). A feedback element starts with a type octet whose 3-bit Code is either 0, meaning a Size octet follows, or 1 to 7, giving the total size in octets of the feedback data and CID field. The Acktype value 3 is reserved and MUST NOT be used.

Feedback can be interspersed with other packets or piggybacked on them, and several elements can be concatenated in one packet. This RFC fixes the interoperability issue from RFC 4995: the Size field counts the FEEDBACK data and the CID field together, in octets.

Segmentation lets a compressor split a packet that is too large for the channel. It is not particularly efficient, and link-layer segmentation SHOULD be used instead when available. It assumes in-order delivery, and if that cannot be guaranteed, ROHC segmentation MUST NOT be used. The segments are rebuilt into a reconstructed unit that ends with a 32-bit CRC and must not exceed the channel parameter MRRU, otherwise the unit is discarded. If MRRU is negotiated to be 0, segmentation MUST NOT be used.

Profile 0x0000 (UNCOMPRESSED) sends IP packets without compressing them. After initialization its only overhead is the CID. The compressor initializes it with IR packets, and the only feedback it defines is an ACK.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can wave back to say all is fine or that it got confused. Very big parcels can be cut into pieces, and a plain, unshrunk mode exists for when shrinking is not possible.

sections.title: CRCs and Variable-Length Values
sections.content:
ROHC uses four CRCs, all computed with the algorithm of RFC 1662 and an initial register of all ones. They let the decompressor check its work and notice context damage, which happens when its context no longer matches the compressor's.

  • The 8-bit CRC in IR and IR-DYN headers MUST cover at least the start of the header through the Profile field. It does not let the decompressor verify a full decompression, but it is enough to update the context from the header.
  • The 3-bit CRC in compressed headers is computed over the whole original header. It is too weak to repair a context from a single header, so profiles should not allow decompression with it when the context is assumed invalid.
  • The 7-bit CRC is strong enough that one verified header can validate a repair.
  • The 32-bit CRC verifies a segmented, reconstructed unit.

Many values are sent with a self-describing variable-length encoding. The first bits of the first octet give the length: 0 means 1 octet (7 bits, up to 127), 10 means 2 octets (14 bits, up to 16383), 110 means 3 octets and 111 means 4 octets (29 bits, up to 536870911).
sections.plainLanguage: A CRC is a tiny check number, like counting the pieces after unpacking a box. If the count does not match, something went wrong along the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encryption removes the redundancy that header compression exploits, so there is some pressure to leave headers unencrypted on low-bandwidth links. A malfunctioning or malicious compressor could make the decompressor rebuild packets that do not match the originals but still have valid headers and possibly valid transport checksums. End-to-end authentication and integrity mechanisms are unaffected by compression and can catch this, and ROHC's internal checksum also lowers the chance of unnoticed mismatches.

Denial of service is possible if an intruder injects bogus IR, IR-DYN or feedback packets onto the link and reduces compression efficiency. The RFC notes that an intruder able to inject arbitrary packets at the link layer raises additional security issues that dwarf those of header compression.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks fake notes into the pile, the shortcuts stop working well. But anyone who can do that can cause far bigger trouble.

sections.title: The Profile Identifier Registry
sections.content:
RFC 3095 created an IANA registry of ROHC profile identifiers. Because only the 8 least significant bits are used in packets, two identifiers with identical low 8 bits should be assigned only when the higher-numbered one is meant to supersede the lower. The policy is Specification Required. In the low 8 bits, 0 to 127 is reserved for IETF Standards Track specifications, 128 to 254 is available for other specifications, and 255 is reserved for future extensibility.

The RFC lists the identifiers allocated so far, including 0x0000 for ROHC uncompressed, 0x0001 to 0x0003 for RTP, UDP and ESP from RFC 3095, 0x0006 for ROHC TCP from RFC 4996, and the ROHCv2 profiles 0x0101 to 0x0104 from RFC 5225. This document requires no additional IANA action.
sections.plainLanguage: Every shortcut method gets its own ID number from a central list, so nobody picks the same number twice.
